title: Unseen poetry: comparing two poems
specPoints: Paper 2 Section C: unseen poetry, Question 27.2
AO2: comparing the effects of methods

tips.title: Eight marks, AO2 only
tips.body: Question 27.2 compares methods and their effects. About ten minutes, two paragraphs.

tips.title: Compare the turns
tips.body: Where each poem changes, how suddenly, and in which direction: quick to see, rich to write.

tips.title: Every sentence compares
tips.body: A method in both poems, joined by whereas, while or unlike, and what the difference does.

tips.title: End on a judgement
tips.body: Level 4 is critical: say which poem's method is stronger or more consoling, and why.

why.matters: Comparing two poems you have never seen, in ten minutes, trains the fastest kind of close reading: noticing what two writers do differently with the same idea. It is worth eight marks, and it is also how people compare any two pieces of writing, two reports, two speeches, two reviews. Practising on poems out of copyright lets you read them whole, as the exam will print them.

examples.title: Two reviews of one film
examples.body: Two critics can describe the same film and leave readers with opposite feelings, through the words they choose and where they put the turn. Comparing methods, not opinions, is how you see why.

examples.title: Two speeches on one day
examples.body: On a day of remembrance, two speakers can both mention birdsong and silence and mean different things: one consolation, one grief. The unseen comparison asks you to hear that difference in the choices.

steps.title: Question 27.2: eight marks for methods
steps.body:
After the 24-mark question on the first poem, Question 27.2 prints a second poem on a related idea and asks what the similarities and/or differences are between the methods the two poets use.

**AO2 only.** The mark scheme gives 8 marks in four levels: 7 to 8 for a critical, insightful comparison of the poems with analytical comparison of the effects of methods; 5 to 6 for thoughtful comparison; down to 1 to 2 for a simple comment on one or both poems and identification of methods.

**Methods, not meanings.** 27.2 does not ask you to retell what either poem says. It asks how each poet presents the shared idea, and what is the same or different about how.

**June 2024.** The second poem was *A Day in Autumn*; the question named the shared idea, daily life and connecting with the natural world, and the indicative content suggested connections such as the use of household tasks in both poems and word choices for the beauty of nature.

**Time.** About ten minutes: one or two paragraphs.

steps.title: The second poem: The Darkling Thrush
steps.body:
Thomas Hardy's poem is dated December 1900, at the end of a century. Read it as the second unseen poem, beside *Adlestrop*.

> I leant upon a coppice gate\
>  When Frost was spectre-gray,\
> And Winter’s dregs made desolate\
>  The weakening eye of day.\
> The tangled bine-stems scored the sky\
>  Like strings from broken lyres,\
> And all mankind that haunted nigh\
>  Had sought their household fires.
>
> The land’s sharp features seemed to be\
>  The Century’s corpse outleant,\
> His crypt the cloudy canopy,\
>  The wind his death-lament.\
> The ancient pulse of germ and birth\
>  Was shrunken hard and dry,\
> And every spirit upon earth\
>  Seemed fervourless as I.
>
> At once a voice outburst among\
>  The bleak twigs overhead\
> In a full-hearted evensong\
>  Of joy illimited;\
> An aged thrush, frail, gaunt, and small,\
>  In blast-beruffled plume,\
> Had chosen thus to fling his soul\
>  Upon the growing gloom.
>
> So little cause for carollings\
>  Of such ecstatic sound\
> Was written on terrestrial things\
>  Afar or nigh around,\
> That I could think there trembled through\
>  His happy good-night air\
> Some blessed Hope, whereof he knew\
>  And I was unaware.

**The first half is bleak.** “When Frost was spectre-gray”; “And Winter's dregs made desolate The weakening eye of day”; the tangled bine-stems are “Like strings from broken lyres”; the landscape is “The Century's corpse outleant”. The speaker is “Seemed fervourless as I”.

**The turn.** “At once a voice outburst among The bleak twigs overhead”: “In a full-hearted evensong Of joy illimited”. The singer is “An aged thrush, frail, gaunt, and small”, and has chosen “Had chosen thus to fling his soul Upon the growing gloom”.

**The ending.** The speaker cannot see a reason for the song, and wonders if the bird knows “Some blessed Hope, whereof he knew And I was unaware”.

steps.title: Comparing the methods, not the stories
steps.body: A question in the 27.2 shape: *In both poems the speakers describe a moment when birdsong changes how they see the world. What are the similarities and/or differences between the methods the poets use to present this moment?*

visuals.problem: Plan a 27.2 comparison of Adlestrop and The Darkling Thrush.

steps.text: Similarity: both poems build a still, empty scene and then turn on a bird's song.

Setting before the song: Thomas uses silence and small sounds, “The steam hissed. Someone cleared his throat.” “No one left and no one came”; Hardy uses images of death and decay, “The Century's corpse outleant”.
steps.note: Different methods for the before: absence against deathliness.

steps.text: The turn: Thomas's is quiet, “And for that minute a blackbird sang Close by”; Hardy's is sudden, “At once a voice outburst among The bleak twigs overhead”.
steps.note: The verbs mark the difference: sang against outburst.

steps.text: After the song: Thomas widens the scene to “Of Oxfordshire and Gloucestershire”; Hardy turns inward to doubt, “Some blessed Hope, whereof he knew And I was unaware”.
steps.note: Opposite movements: outward to the land, inward to the speaker.

steps.text: Form: Thomas's plain quatrains and short sentences; Hardy's regular eight-line stanzas with a steady rhyme, like a hymn.

steps.title: Methods to compare quickly
steps.body:
In ten minutes there is room for two or three comparisons. These are the quickest to see and the richest to write about.

**Structure and the turn.** Where each poem changes, and how suddenly.

**Imagery.** What each poet compares things to: Hardy's corpse, crypt and broken lyres; Thomas's clouds and haycocks.

**Sound and sentence.** Short sentences and caesura against long flowing sentences.

**Form.** Stanza length, rhyme, regularity: Hardy's eight-line stanzas with alternating rhyme; Thomas's quatrains with lighter rhyme.

**Endings.** Where each poem leaves the reader: in a place, or in a question.

steps.title: Hardy's methods in close-up
steps.body:
**Personified winter.** “When Frost was spectre-gray”; winter's dregs; the eye of day weakening. The season is a dying person.

**A century's death.** The land is “The Century's corpse outleant”, the clouds his crypt, the wind his death-lament: an extended metaphor for the end of 1900.

**Religious words for the song.** An *evensong* is an evening church service; the bird sings “In a full-hearted evensong Of joy illimited”; the ending names “Some blessed Hope, whereof he knew And I was unaware”. The song is heard as something like faith.

**Contrast.** “An aged thrush, frail, gaunt, and small”: the most unlikely singer. “So little cause for carollings”: the joy has no visible reason.

**Form.** Eight-line stanzas, alternating longer and shorter lines, a steady rhyme: the regular music of a hymn.

steps.title: Writing 27.2 in ten minutes
steps.body:
**One sentence of similarity,** one of difference, then develop.

**Every sentence names a method in both poems.** *Both*, *whereas*, *while*, *unlike*.

**Say what the difference does.** Not only *Thomas uses short sentences and Hardy long ones*, but *so Thomas's moment is a pause and Hardy's a flood*.

**Use short quotations.** A word or phrase from each.

**Do not re-analyse the first poem at length.** You did that in 27.1; here, compare.

steps.title: Critical, insightful comparison
steps.body:
Level 4 asks for a critical, insightful comparison of the poems and analytical comparison of the effects of methods.

**Insight: compare the direction of the change.** Both birds change the speaker's world, but Thomas's widens it outward and Hardy's opens a gap inward, between the bird's hope and the speaker's.

**Analytical: compare effects, not features.** Thomas's caesura makes stillness; Hardy's regular hymn-like stanzas make the song sound like a service the speaker attends but cannot join.

**Critical: judge.** Which poem's moment is more certain? Thomas's landscape is fully present; Hardy's Hope is only guessed at. The judgement is where the answer becomes critical.

questions.prompt: In both 'Adlestrop' and 'The Darkling Thrush', the speakers describe a moment when birdsong changes how they see the world. What are the similarities and/or differences between the methods the poets use to present this moment?
questions.solution: Both poets build a still scene and turn it on a bird's song, but the methods take the change in opposite directions. Thomas makes stillness out of small sounds and absence: “The steam hissed. Someone cleared his throat.” “No one left and no one came”. Hardy makes it out of death: the landscape is “The Century's corpse outleant”, and the speaker is “Seemed fervourless as I”. The turns differ in force. Thomas's is gentle and late, “And for that minute a blackbird sang Close by”; Hardy's is sudden and halfway, “At once a voice outburst among The bleak twigs overhead”, and his religious diction, “In a full-hearted evensong Of joy illimited”, gives the song the weight of a service. After the song, Thomas's lines widen outward, “mistier, Farther and farther, all the birds”, ending in the open space of “Of Oxfordshire and Gloucestershire”; Hardy's turn inward, to “Some blessed Hope, whereof he knew And I was unaware”. Thomas's moment is complete, a landscape heard; Hardy's is incomplete, a hope he can only guess at, and so the older poem is less consoling, though perhaps the more honest.

questions.prompt: In 'The Darkling Thrush', how does the poet present feelings about hope? Write an opening idea and two paragraphs.
questions.solution:
Hardy presents hope as something heard in the world but not felt by the speaker: it belongs to the bird, and he can only guess at it. The first half builds a landscape without hope. Winter is personified, “When Frost was spectre-gray”, the day's eye is weakening, the tangled bine-stems are “Like strings from broken lyres”, and in an extended metaphor the whole land is “The Century's corpse outleant”, a dead century laid out in its crypt of cloud. The speaker includes himself: every spirit “Seemed fervourless as I”.

The turn is sudden: “At once a voice outburst among The bleak twigs overhead”, and the song is “In a full-hearted evensong Of joy illimited”, a religious word for a joy without limit. The singer is “An aged thrush, frail, gaunt, and small”, and has chosen “Had chosen thus to fling his soul Upon the growing gloom”; the joy is an act of will against the gloom. Yet the speaker finds “So little cause for carollings”, and ends on “Some blessed Hope, whereof he knew And I was unaware”. Perhaps the hope is real and simply hidden from him; perhaps it is only the bird's. Either way, Hardy lets hope exist in the poem while keeping the speaker outside it.

examTechnique.body:
**27.2: 8 marks, AO2.** Compare methods and their effects.

**Open with a similarity and a difference.**

**Two methods, both poems, every sentence.**

**End on a judgement.** Say which poem's method makes the moment stronger, or more consoling, and why. About ten minutes, after about thirty-five on 27.1.
examinerErrors: Writing only about the second poem.
Comparing subjects or seasons, not methods.
Re-analysing the first poem at length.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer to 27.2 compares the direction and force of each poem's change, analyses the effects of the same methods in both, uses a short quotation from each, and ends on a critical judgement, in about ten minutes.
